facts.fact_text: On 4 July 2002 the applicant organised a demonstration aimed at forcing the authorities to preserve the ballot papers of the 2002 legislative elections with a view to a potential recounting.

The demonstration organised by the applicant on 4 July 2002 consisted of completely blocking all six lanes of Erzsébet Bridge, a centrally situated bridge over the Danube, by parking six cars across it with their doors locked.
The demonstrators, including the applicant, refused to comply with the police's order to remove the vehicles and leave Erzsébet Bridge.
On 5 July 2002 the Pest Central District Court imposed a regulatory fine of 50,000 Hungarian forints on the applicant.
On 16 June 2008 the applicant was convicted of 'disturbance of public works' within the meaning of section 260(1) of the Criminal Code.
The applicant was sentenced to 30 days of community work by the Pest Central District Court.

The Pest Central District Court held that the applicant, by not complying with the police's instruction to leave the site of the demonstration, had committed the regulatory offence of disorderly conduct within the meaning of section 142(1c) of Act no. LXIX on Regulatory Offences.
On 16 June 2008 the applicant was convicted of 'disturbance of public works' within the meaning of section 260(1) of the Criminal Code.

Section 260(1) of the Criminal Code, as in force at the relevant time, provided that any person who interferes with the functioning of public works to a considerable extent by damaging their equipment, cables or interfering with them in any other way, is guilty of a felony punishable by imprisonment of up to five years.

Section 260(4) of the Criminal Code, as in force at the relevant time, provided that for the purposes of section 260, 'public works' shall mean public utilities, public transportation operations, telecommunications networks, as well as plants producing war materials, energy or basic materials designed for industrial use.
The Pest Central District Court observed that the demonstration on 4 July 2002 had caused traffic to become paralysed all over Budapest for several hours.

The Pest Central District Court observed that the demonstration on 4 July 2002 disturbed the running of 29 bus lines in respect of 642 scheduled individual bus trips, concerning approximately 23,000 passengers.
On 2 July 2002, Parliament had decided not to put on the agenda a bill for the amendment of the 90-day statutory preservation period of the ballot papers.

International observers, in particular the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), found that the 2002 parliamentary elections in Hungary had been conducted in a manner consistent with international standards.

The Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) found that the Hungarian electoral system had provided the basis for a generally transparent, accountable, free, fair and equal process in the 2002 parliamentary elections.

The Pest Central District Court held that the applicant's action on 4 July 2002 could not be regarded as a spontaneous and prompt response to an event, as the court was satisfied that the statutory date for ballot paper destruction was 20 July 2002 as per Decree no. 48/2001.

The Budapest Regional Court noted that 'the message of the judgment is not that non-notified assemblies cannot be peaceful; the message is that an assembly, notified or non-notified, is not peaceful where, by its very manner, it constitutes unlawful conduct.'
The Budapest Regional Court held that an assembly may be rendered non-peaceful by passive conduct.

The Budapest Regional Court held that the accused parties' conduct, which in its outward appearance seemed to be peaceful, was rendered non-peaceful by its causal result — the major disturbance of road traffic — and was thereby not protected under the law.

Section 1 of Act no. V of 1991 on Certain Amnesty Measures provided that in connection with the road blockades paralysing the country's life from 25 to 28 October 1990, no criminal proceedings shall be instituted or conducted for the disturbance of public works under section 260 of the Criminal Code.
